## 제1인터내셔널과 독일 사회민주주의자들의 반전 {uk germany france}

제2제정은 전쟁 전부터 국제노동자협회를 적으로 대했다. 1870년 5월 국민투표 전날 정부는 「황제 암살 음모를 꾸미는 비밀결사」라는 구실로 파리·리옹·루앙·마르세유·브레스트의 협회 운영위원들을 일제히 검거했고, 6월 22일부터 7월 5일까지 열린 재판에서 음모 혐의는 근거 없음이 드러났지만 여러 회원이 사회주의 신념만으로 투옥되었다. 프랑스 지부들이 국민투표는 「국내의 전제와 국외의 전쟁」에 찬성하는 표라고 호소한 결과 대도시 노동자들은 거의 한 몸처럼 반대표를 던졌으나, 농촌의 표가 균형을 뒤집었다. 전쟁 위기가 닥치자 파리의 협회 회원들은 7월 12일 『레베유』에 「모든 나라의 노동자에게」라는 선언을 실어 「우위나 왕조를 위한 전쟁은 노동자의 눈에 범죄적 부조리일 뿐」이라며 「독일의 형제들이여, 우리의 분열은 라인강 양쪽에서 전제의 완전한 승리로 끝날 뿐」이라고 썼다. 뇌이쉬르센 등 여러 지역 선언이 뒤따랐고, 경찰청장 피에트리는 교외 노동자들의 평화 시위가 커지자 거리 정치를 모두 금지했다. 독일에서도 7월 16일 브라운슈바이크의 노동자 대중집회가 파리 선언에 전적으로 동의하며 「우리는 모든 전쟁, 특히 왕조 전쟁의 적」이라고 결의했고, 켐니츠에서는 작센 노동자 5만 명을 대표하는 대의원 회의가 이 전쟁을 「오로지 왕조적인」 전쟁으로 규정했으며, 베를린 지부는 「나팔 소리도 대포 소리도, 승리도 패배도 우리를 공동의 과업에서 떼어 놓지 못한다」고 답했다. [25](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1871/civil-war-france/ch01.htm)

런던의 총평의회는 7월 23일 카를 마르크스가 쓴 첫 번째 담화를 냈다. 담화는 1870년 7월의 「전쟁 음모」를 1851년 12월 쿠데타의 「개정판」이라 부르고, 「제2제정의 조종은 이미 파리에서 울렸다. 그것은 시작했던 대로 희극으로 끝날 것」이라고 예언했다. 독일 쪽에서는 방어 전쟁이지만 독일을 그 처지로 몰아넣은 것은 보나파르트와 공모해 국내의 반대를 억누르고 독일을 호엔촐레른 왕조에 병합하려 한 비스마르크의 프로이센이며, 독일 노동계급이 이 전쟁이 「엄격히 방어적인 성격」을 잃고 프랑스 인민에 대한 전쟁으로 타락하도록 둔다면 승리든 패배든 똑같이 재앙이 되리라고 경고했다. 배후에는 러시아가 있으니 프로이센 정부가 「코사크의 도움」을 받는 순간 독일은 정당한 동정을 잃는다고도 썼다. 북독일연방 제국의회에서는 사회민주노동자당(아이제나흐파)의 두 의원 아우구스트 베벨과 빌헬름 리프크네히트가 7월 21일(독일어 출처는 19일) 전쟁 공채 표결에서 기권했다. 프로이센 정부를 지지하지도 나폴레옹을 편드는 것으로 보이지도 않으려고 베벨이 고안한 타협이었다. 파리 선언에 호응한 브라운슈바이크에 있던 당 중앙위원회의 빌헬름 브라케와 자무엘 슈피어는 마르크스처럼 전쟁의 첫 단계를 공격에 맞선 정당한 방어로 보아 「형제에 대한 전쟁」을 거부한 두 의원과 격렬하게 부딪쳤고, 창당 1년 된 당은 깨질 뻔했다. 스당 뒤 브라운슈바이크 위원회도 전쟁 계속에 반대로 돌아섰다. 마르크스와 엥겔스는 9월 1일 무렵 위원회에 보낸 편지에서 알자스-로렌 병합이 독일을 영원히 전쟁에서 지켜 주리라는 주장을 뒤집어, 병합은 「이 전쟁을 유럽의 제도로 만드는 최선의 수단」이며 「서쪽의 폴란드」를 붙들어 두기 위해 새 독일에 군사 전제를 영속시키고, 다가올 강화를 「프랑스가 잃은 영토를 되찾을 만큼 회복할 때까지의 휴전」으로 만들 것이라고 썼다. 9월 5일 위원회는 선언을 내어 「우리는 알자스와 로렌의 병합에 항의한다. 우리는 독일 노동계급의 이름으로 말하고 있음을 안다」며 프랑스 공화국과의 「명예로운 강화」와 루이 보나파르트의 인도를 요구했다. 사령관 포겔 폰 팔켄슈타인 장군의 명령으로 선언문은 압수되었고 위원 전원과 인쇄공까지 체포되어 「보통 범죄자처럼 쇠사슬에 묶여」 브라운슈바이크에서 1,000km 떨어진 동프로이센의 뢰첸으로 끌려갔다. 마르크스는 9월 15일 『폴 몰 가제트』에 이 사실을 알렸다. 자유주의자 요한 야코비도 병합에 반대하다 투옥되었다. 9월 9일 총평의회의 두 번째 담화는 「방어 전쟁은 사실상 루이 보나파르트의 항복, 스당의 항복, 파리의 공화국 선포로 끝났다」고 선언하고, 「물질적 보장」을 내세우는 병합론을 조목조목 반박하며 「군사적 고려를 국경의 원칙으로 삼는 것」은 「새 전쟁의 씨앗」을 품는다고 썼다. 프랑스를 러시아의 품에 밀어 넣는 병합은 「슬라브 민족과 로망스 민족과의 전쟁」을 부르리라는 경고였다. 담화는 공화국을 환영하면서도 오를레앙파가 군대와 경찰을 쥐었다고 경계했으며, 프랑스 노동자에게 적이 파리 문 앞에 있는 지금 정부 전복 시도는 「절망적인 어리석음」이니 공화국의 자유를 계급 조직에 쓰라고 당부했다. 11월 26일 북독일연방 제국의회가 추가 전쟁 공채를 다룰 때 베벨과 리프크네히트는 「프랑스 영토의 어떤 병합도 포기하는」 강화 제안을 내놓고 공채에 반대표를 던졌다. 토론은 두 의원에 대한 반역 비난으로 번졌고, 소란과 특히 리프크네히트를 겨냥한 폭행이 뒤따랐다. 12월 17일 두 사람은 당 기관지 『폴크스슈타트』의 둘째 편집자 아돌프 헤프너와 함께 체포되었다. 리프크네히트는 프로이센 주도의 통일을 「이 체제에는 한 사람도, 한 푼도 주지 않는다」는 구호로 맞았고, 이 말은 비스마르크 국가에 대한 당의 반대를 상징하는 표어가 되었다. 1871년 3월 3일 새 독일 제국의회 선거에서 베벨이 당선되자 정부는 압력에 밀려 3월 28일 세 사람을 일단 풀어 주었다. 베벨은 제국의회에서 파리 코뮌을 국제 노동계급이 치를 긴 싸움의 「전초전」이라 불렀다. 전쟁이 끝나 국가반역죄(Landesverrat)로는 재판할 수 없게 되자 비스마르크는 내란죄(Hochverrat)로 바꿔 기소를 밀어붙였다. 1872년 3월 11일부터 26일까지 라이프치히 배심법원에서 열린 재판에서 헤프너는 무죄, 베벨과 리프크네히트는 유죄 정족수인 배심원 8명의 찬성으로 유죄가 되어 요새금고 2년을 선고받았고 베벨의 의원직은 박탈되었다. 리프크네히트는 법정에서 스스로를 「혁명의 병사」라 불렀고, 검찰이 『공산당 선언』을 조서에 올린 덕에 절판되었던 이 책을 합법적으로 다시 펴낼 수 있게 되었다. 1873년 1월 보궐선거에서 베벨은 첫 선거보다 4,000표 넘게 더 얻어 다시 당선되었다. ## 베르사유의 제국 선포와 휴전 {germany france}

8월과 9월의 승리는 남독일 군주들을 북독일연방으로 끌어들였다. 1870년 11월 바덴·헤센·뷔르템베르크·바이에른이 조약을 맺었고, 12월 8일 연방 참의원은 연방의 이름을 「독일 제국」으로 바꾸고 프로이센 왕을 독일 황제로 삼기로 했으며, 9~10일 제국의회가 황제 칭호를 바치기로 의결했다. 새 헌법은 1871년 1월 1일 발효했다. 빌헬름 1세는 황제 칭호가 프로이센 왕의 칭호를 가릴까 꺼렸고 「독일의 황제(Kaiser von Deutschland)」를 원했으나, 비스마르크는 남독일 군주들과 오스트리아 황제가 반발할 것이라며 「독일 황제」로 정했다. 선포일은 1701년 프로이센 초대 왕의 대관 기념일인 1월 18일로 잡았다. 그날 베르사유 궁전 거울의 방에는 각 연대 대표단이 전투로 찢긴 군기를 들고 들어찼고, 한가운데 옥좌 대신 야전 제단을 놓고 예배를 올린 뒤 비스마르크가 선포문을 읽었다. 빌헬름의 유일한 사위 바덴 대공 프리드리히가 헌법상 칭호를 피해 「빌헬름 황제 폐하」를 외쳤고 참석자들이 세 번 따라 외쳤다. 빌헬름은 종교적 성격을 강조했고, 비스마르크는 황제가 제후들 위에 서지 않고 스스로를 전우들과 함께 승리한 사령관으로 여겼다고 공공연히 비판했다. 포위된 적국 수도의 궁전에서 치러진 이 의식은 프랑스에 국가적 굴욕으로 기억되었다. 겨울 동안 독일 수뇌부의 긴장도 커졌다. 몰트케와 블루멘탈은 외곽 요새를 차례로 무너뜨리는 체계적 공성을, 비스마르크는 신속한 종전을 원했고, 긴 포위가 경제를 짓누르고 프랑스에 새 군대를 만들 시간을 주며 중립국을 끌어들일 것을 걱정했다. 1월 25일 빌헬름 1세는 몰트케를 눌러 앞으로 모든 작전을 비스마르크와 상의하라고 명했고, 비스마르크는 곧바로 대구경 크루프 공성포로 시내를 포격하게 했다. 1월 23일 각료회의에서 전면 휴전 교섭의 권한을 받은 파브르는 그날 저녁 베르사유로 갔다. 비스마르크는 국민방위군이 봉기할까 걱정하는 그에게 「봉기를 도발하라, 아직 그것을 진압할 군대가 있을 때」라고 조언했다. 합의된 조건은 파리 외곽 요새의 인도, 1개 사단을 뺀 정규군의 무장해제, 국민방위군의 무장 유지, 2억 프랑의 배상금, 2월 19일까지의 휴전과 국민의회 선거였다. 27일 자정 파리에서 포성이 멎었고, 28일 파브르와 비스마르크가 휴전 협정에 서명했다. 쥐라·두·코트도르 세 주는 벨포르 공성을 유지하려는 프랑스 측 요청으로 휴전에서 제외되었다. 파브르는 보르도 정부에 이를 알리지 않았고, 이 지역에서 작전 중이던 클랭샹 휘하의 동부군은 휴전을 믿고 멈췄다가 만토이펠의 남부군에 포위되었다. 2월 1일 8만 7천 명의 마지막 프랑스군은 퐁타를리에에서 레베리에르를 거쳐 스위스로 넘어가 무장해제되고 억류되었다. 국민방위군이 무기를 간직한 것은 뒤에 파리 코뮌 봉기를 가능하게 했다. 보르도의 강베타는 1월 29일 전보로 항복 소식을 받고 격분해 받아들이지 않았다. 2월 6일 강베타는 사임하고 지방 군대의 지휘권을 정부에 넘겼다. 2월 8일 43개 주가 점령된 가운데 치른 국민의회 선거는 모든 공공 집회가 금지되어 파리에서만 선거운동이 가능했고, 강화를 약속한 정통왕조파와 오를레앙파가 큰 다수를 얻었다. 강베타는 8개 주에서 당선되었지만, 티에르는 여러 선거구(출처에 따라 23곳 또는 86곳)에서 동시에 뽑혔다. 2월 12일 보르도에 모인 의회는 티에르를 행정 수반으로 세웠고, 19일 의원들은 공화정이냐 왕정이냐를 묻지 않기로 하는 「보르도 협약」을 맺었다. 2월 26일 베르사유에서 가조약이 서명되었고, 3월 1일 프로이센·바이에른·작센 병사 3만 명이 검은 천을 두른 침묵의 파리에서 승전 행진을 한 뒤 이틀 만에 동쪽 교외로 물러났다. 같은 날 국민의회는 황제의 폐위를 공식 선언하고 패전의 책임을 그에게 돌렸다. 강화가 이루어지자 비스마르크는 나폴레옹 3세를 풀어 주었고, 그는 3월 20일 영국으로 건너가 켄트의 치즐허스트에 자리 잡았다가 1873년 1월 9일 방광 결석 수술 끝에 죽었다. 마지막 말은 「스당에서 우리가 비겁하지 않았던 게 사실이지?」였다고 한다. ## 프랑크푸르트 조약과 알자스-로렌 {france germany}

1871년 5월 10일 프랑크푸르트에서 독일 제국과 프랑스 공화국이 강화 조약에 서명했다. 프랑스는 알자스의 바랭·오랭 두 주를 벨포르와 그 주변을 빼고, 로렌에서는 모젤 주의 대부분과 샤토살랭·사르부르를 포함한 뫼르트 주의 3분의 1, 보주 주의 살과 시르메크 칸톤을 넘겼다. 마을과 도시 1,694곳, 144만 7천 헥타르, 주민 159만 7천 명이었고, 프랑스는 광업과 제철 잠재력의 20%를 잃었다. 병합지 주민에게는 1872년 10월 1일까지 프랑스 국적을 지키고 이주할지 남아서 독일 국민이 될지 선택할 권리가 주어졌다. 배상금은 금 50억 프랑으로 5년 안에 갚아야 했고 1871년에 10억 프랑을 먼저 내야 독일군이 철수를 시작했으며, 완납까지 프랑스 일부가 점령되었다. 이 액수는 인구 비례로 나폴레옹 1세가 1807년 프로이센에 물린 배상금과 똑같이 맞춘 것이었다. 프랑스는 빌헬름 1세의 독일 황제 즉위를 인정했다. 프랑스는 기한보다 빨리 배상금을 치렀고, 독일군은 1873년 9월 물러났다. 독일 군부는 보주 산맥까지의 알자스와 티옹빌에서 메스에 이르는 길목을 미래의 프랑스와의 전쟁에 대비한 필수 지역으로 보았고. 새 국경은 대체로 언어 경계를 따랐지만 프랑스어권 메스의 병합은 프랑스에서 분노를 일으켰고, 철과 석탄 같은 자원은 병합의 동기로 작용하지 않은 것으로 보인다. [35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Frankfurt_%281871%29) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War)

병합지는 1871년 6월 28일 「제국령 알자스-로렌」이 되어 연방 구성국이 아니라 황제가 임명한 총독이 다스리는 직할 영토가 되었다. 프로이센은 주민을 먼저 「독일화」해야 한다고 보아 처음에는 점령지처럼 다루었다. 주민의 약 90%가 독일어 방언을 썼지만 가톨릭 신자들은 개신교 프로이센 주도의 통일을 의심했고, 1872~73년 문화투쟁이 이 지역에 미치자 가톨릭 교회는 저항의 통로가 되었다. 프랑스 국적을 택한 사람은 160,878명으로 전체의 10.4%였고 오랭에서는 20.3%에 이르렀으나, 실제로 프랑스로 떠난 사람은 약 5만 명이었다. 일부 추정은 선택자를 28만 명, 이주자를 13만 명까지 잡는다. 1874년 이 지역에 제국의회 의석 15석이 주어지자 당선자 가운데 6~10명이 병합에 반대하는 「항의 의원」이었고, 이들은 「의견을 묻지 않고 프랑크푸르트 조약으로 독일 제국에 편입된 알자스-로렌 주민에게 이 병합에 대한 의견을 표명할 기회를 달라」는 프랑스어 동의안을 냈으나 큰 표차로 부결되었다. 1918년 프랑스로 돌아갈 때도 주민 투표는 없었다. 비스마르크가 병합을 원했는지, 군부와 여론의 물결에 떠밀렸는지는 역사가들 사이에서 논쟁거리다. 비스마르크의 전기 작가들은 그가 「마지못해 양보했다」고 보며, 병합을 그의 가장 큰 실책으로 꼽는다. 프랑스를 영구적인 적으로 만들었기 때문이다. [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace%E2%80%93Lorraine) [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck) [35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Frankfurt_%281871%29)

독일은 장교 33,101명과 병사 1,113,254명을 프랑스에 보내 전투에서 28,306명을 잃었고(전사 17,585명, 부상으로 사망 10,721명), 병으로 12,147명이 더 죽었는데 장티푸스 사망자만 6,965명이었다. 부상자는 89,732명이었다. 프랑스의 전투 사망자는 77,000명(전사 41,000명, 부상 사망 36,000명)이고 병사(病死)가 45,000명을 넘어 총 사망자는 138,871명이었으며, 부상자 137,626명, 포로 383,860명에 더해 90,192명이 스위스에, 6,300명이 벨기에에 억류되었다. 프로이센군의 포로 처형(도르나흐에서 프랑스 병사 200명 이상)과 민간인 폭력도 기록되었다. 전쟁은 끝났지만 파리의 싸움은 끝나지 않았다. 포위 중 노동자 구역의 국민방위군은 장교를 선출하고 정부 명령을 거부할 만큼 정치화되어 있었고, 1871년 3월 18일 정규군이 몽마르트르의 대포를 거두려 하자 저항하며 장군 둘을 죽였다. 정부와 군은 베르사유로 물러났고 파리에는 코뮌이 섰다. 5월 21~28일 「피의 주간」에 정규군이 파리를 되찾았고, 정부군이 죽인 코뮌 가담자는 7천에서 3만 명으로 추산되다가 묘지 매장 기록을 조사한 최근 연구에서는 6천에서 1만 명으로 잡힌다. 생존자들은 1880년 강베타가 낸 법안으로 사면되었다. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_Versailles)

## 평가 {france germany}

전쟁의 원인을 둘러싼 서술은 지금도 갈린다. 비스마르크 자신이 회고록에서 「프랑스와의 전쟁은 자연히 오스트리아와의 전쟁에 뒤따른다고 늘 생각했다」고 써서 치밀한 계획의 신화를 키웠고, 일부 역사가는 그가 남독일 국가들을 끌어들이려고 일부러 프랑스를 자극했다고 본다. 반면 엠스 전보가 전쟁의 원인으로 한 역할은 사소했으며 나폴레옹 3세가 이기리라 믿고 이미 전쟁을 택했다는 견해가 있고, 프랑스 역사가 프랑수아 로트와 피에르 밀자는 황제가 호전적 언론과 여론에 떠밀렸다고 본다. 독일에서는 전쟁의 성격을 둘러싼 논쟁이 있다. 토비아스 아란트는 스당까지의 전쟁을 고전적 「내각 전쟁」으로 보고, 그 뒤 국방정부의 민간인 동원과 병합 요구로 전쟁이 변질되었다고 한다. 알렉산더 자이퍼트는 후방의 동원과 선전을 근거로 이 전쟁을 20세기 총력전으로 가는 한 단계로 분류하지만, 크리스티네 크뤼거는 후방은 총력전의 여러 특징 가운데 하나일 뿐이며 포로를 인도적으로 다루고 세계대전과 달리 비교적 빨리 대결을 끝낸 점을 들어 반박한다. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_Dispatch) [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck) [24](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsch-Franz%C3%B6sischer_Krieg) [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III)

수치는 출처마다 다르다. 메스에서 항복한 병력은 전쟁 개관 항목이 173,000명, 메스 포위 항목이 193,000명(장교 6,000명과 병사 167,000명이 포로가 되고 환자 2만 명이 남았다)으로 적는다. 그라블로트의 프랑스군 병력은 112,800명이지만 나폴레옹 3세 항목은 메스에 갇힌 바젠의 군대를 175,000명으로 쓴다. 알자스-로렌에서 프랑스 국적을 택한 사람은 공식 집계 160,878명과 최대 28만 명의 추정이 나란히 있다. 1871년 2월 선거에서 티에르가 당선된 선거구는 23곳 또는 86곳으로 나오고, 베벨과 리프크네히트의 전쟁 공채 기권일은 영어 출처가 7월 21일, 독일어 출처가 7월 19일이며, 두 사람의 체포 시점을 영어 베벨 항목은 1871년 12월로 적지만 리프크네히트 항목과 독일어 재판 항목은 1870년 12월 17일로 적는다. 코뮌 희생자는 7천에서 3만 명이라는 전통적 추정과 6천에서 1만 명이라는 매장 기록 연구가 맞선다. 이 글은 각 지점에서 범위를 함께 적었다. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Metz_%281870%29) [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III) [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace%E2%80%93Lorraine) [34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1871_French_legislative_election) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Gambetta) [26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bebel) [27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Liebknecht) [31](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipziger_Hochverratsprozess)

사회주의 운동에 이 전쟁은 두 가지 선례를 남겼다. 하나는 교전국 양쪽의 노동자 조직이 서로 평화의 인사를 주고받고, 총평의회가 두 차례 담화로 「왕조 전쟁」을 규탄한 뒤 전쟁이 방어의 성격을 잃는 순간 승자의 병합에 반대한 일이다. 마르크스는 독일 노동자의 「물질적 보장」 비판을 넘어, 병합이 프랑스를 러시아의 품에 밀어 넣어 「슬라브 민족과 로망스 민족과의 전쟁」을 부르리라 내다보았고, 통일된 독일 제국을 「의회의 형식으로 가린 군사 전제」라 불렀다. 뒤의 역사가들도 병합을 비스마르크의 가장 큰 실책으로 꼽지만, 복수심(revanchism)이 1880년대에는 가라앉았고 알자스-로렌 회복이 1차 세계대전 개전 뒤에야 프랑스의 전쟁 목표가 되었다고 본다. 다른 하나는 의회에서의 표결이다. 베벨과 리프크네히트의 기권과 반대, 브라운슈바이크 위원회의 쇠사슬, 라이프치히의 요새금고형은 「이 체제에는 한 사람도, 한 푼도」를 독일 사회민주주의의 표어로 만들었고, 1871년 이후 독일 민족주의가 프랑스에 맞서 「제국의 적」(폴란드인·덴마크인·가톨릭·사회민주주의자)을 배제하며 자신을 규정하게 되자 이 표어는 당의 정체성이 되었다. 그러나 같은 베벨이 1913년 재산세를 조건으로 군사 예산에 찬성해 1914년의 전쟁 공채 표결을 예고했듯이, 1870년의 선례는 1914년에 지켜지지 않았다. [25](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1871/civil-war-france/ch01.htm) [18](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1871/civil-war-france/ch02.htm) [37](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_of_Germany) [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Liebknecht) [24](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsch-Franz%C3%B6sischer_Krieg) [26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bebel)

## Europe after 1866 and the road to war {france germany}

When Prussia beat Austria at Königgrätz in 1866 and bound the German states north of the Main into the North German Confederation, the standing of the French Second Empire, the self-declared dominant power of the continent since 1859, was shaken. Prussia annexed Hanover, Schleswig-Holstein, Nassau, Hesse-Kassel and Frankfurt, enlarging its territory by nearly a quarter to a population of about 24 million. France, which had stayed out of the war, gained nothing, and public opinion called for "revenge for Sadowa". Napoleon III demanded a return to the frontiers of 1814 with the annexation of Luxembourg, most of the Saarland and the Bavarian Palatinate; Otto von Bismarck dismissed this as a "tipping policy", refused, and showed the written demands to Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse-Darmstadt, which hastened defensive alliances with the South German states. Bismarck knew that France had to appear as the aggressor if the southern states were to side with Prussia. The constitution of the North German Confederation, in force from July 1867, made the Prussian king its head and Bismarck its chancellor, with a Reichstag elected by universal manhood suffrage; August Bebel of Saxony entered that Reichstag in 1867. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_Dispatch) [3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_German_Confederation)

The immediate occasion was the Spanish throne. After Isabella II was driven out in 1868, the vacant crown was offered to Prince Leopold of the Catholic Sigmaringen branch of the Hohenzollerns; when the candidacy became known on 2 July 1870, the French parliament and press raged against encirclement by Prussia and Spain. Under French pressure Leopold withdrew on 11 July, which was already seen as a diplomatic defeat for Prussia. The foreign minister, the Duc de Gramont, went further and demanded that the Prussian king guarantee that no Hohenzollern would ever again be a candidate. On the morning of 13 July the French ambassador, Vincent Benedetti, stopped Wilhelm I on the promenade at Bad Ems and put the demand to him; the king refused, politely but firmly. Heinrich Abeken reported the conversation by telegram to Bismarck in Berlin, and Bismarck cut the king's conciliatory phrases, reduced the text to the statement that the king had refused to receive the ambassador again and had informed him through an adjutant that he had nothing further to say, and released it that evening to the press and the foreign embassies. The French translation by the Havas agency rendered "Adjutant" as "adjudant", a non-commissioned officer, which implied that the king had deliberately insulted the ambassador. Bismarck said the text would have "the effect of a red rag on the Gallic bull". [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_Dispatch) [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III) [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck)

On 14 July the French papers printed the translation of Bismarck's communiqué, not their ambassador's report. Gramont said he felt he had "just received a slap"; Adolphe Thiers, the monarchist leader in parliament, argued that France had already won the diplomatic battle and had no reason to fight, but was drowned out by cries of "traitor" and "Prussian". The prime minister, Émile Ollivier, said he accepted responsibility for the war "with a light heart", and a crowd of 15,000 to 20,000 marched through Paris demanding war. France ordered mobilisation on the 15th, the North German Confederation mobilised that night, and Bavaria, Baden and Württemberg followed. The legislature voted war credits by an overwhelming majority, and on 19 July France declared war on Prussia. The Second Empire, which had won 7.33 million yes votes in the plebiscite of 8 May and seemed "more popular than ever", went to war without a single ally, hoping that Austria, Denmark and Italy would join in. Historians disagree: some hold that Bismarck deliberately provoked France in order to bring the South German states into the Confederation, others that he exploited events as they unfolded and that Napoleon III had already resolved on war to stabilise his regime. All agree that Bismarck recognised the potential of the new German alliances. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_Dispatch) [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III)

## From the frontier battles to Sedan {france germany}

The difference between the two armies showed in mobilisation. The Prussian General Staff revised its railway mobilisation plans every year, and Helmuth von Moltke, appointed chief of staff for the duration five days after the mobilisation order of 5 July, gained the right to issue orders equivalent to royal commands. The German forces assembled south of Mainz in three armies: the First under Steinmetz, the Second under Prince Friedrich Karl and the Third under the Prussian crown prince Friedrich Wilhelm. On the French side, competing private railway companies and the absence of military control of the lines left reservists and loaded wagons choking the stations, and the army lost 100,000 stragglers before a shot was fired. At the outbreak 462,000 German soldiers stood on the frontier against 270,000 French. The French infantry's Chassepot rifle outranged the Dreyse needle gun, but the Krupp steel breech-loading guns of the Prussian artillery fired farther and faster than the French bronze muzzle-loaders. Napoleon III left for Metz on 28 July to command the "Army of the Rhine", though he was too ill to ride; the brief occupation of Saarbrücken on 2 August was the only French gain on German soil. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmuth_von_Moltke_the_Elder) [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III)

The first action came at Wissembourg on 4 August, where the crown prince's Third Army overwhelmed the isolated division of General Douay, who was killed. On the 6th the armies of Steinmetz and Friedrich Karl drove Frossard's II Corps from the heights of Spicheren, and on the same day at Wörth (Frœschwiller) Marshal MacMahon's 35,000 men fought the 140,000 of the Third Army, lost around 10,000 killed and wounded and 9,200 prisoners, and fell back beyond the Vosges. Marshal Achille Bazaine's Army of the Rhine, about 160,000 strong in the fortress of Metz, tried to withdraw towards Châlons on 15 August, but on the 16th at Mars-la-Tour Alvensleben's III Corps of 30,000 men took Vionville against odds of four to one and blocked the road west; the German official history recorded 15,780 German and 13,761 French casualties. The Battle of Gravelotte-St. Privat on the 18th was the largest of the war: 188,332 men under Moltke attacked the entrenched 112,800 of Bazaine, at a cost of 20,163 German and 12,275 French casualties, and the next day the Army of the Rhine withdrew into Metz, where it was besieged. Apart from attempted break-outs at Noisseville on 31 August and Bellevue on 7 October, Bazaine stayed inside the fortress, and historians have criticised his passivity. On 17 August Napoleon III and MacMahon formed the new Army of Châlons and set out to relieve Bazaine. The army marched north-east towards the Belgian border to avoid the Prussians, but Moltke detached three corps from the siege of Metz to form the Army of the Meuse under the Crown Prince of Saxony, turned north with it and the Third Army, and caught the French at Beaumont on 30 August. Having lost 5,000 men and 40 guns, the Army of Châlons withdrew into the obsolete seventeenth-century fortress of Sedan. On the morning of 1 September the German armies closed the ring on every side. When MacMahon was wounded, command passed through Ducrot to Wimpffen; General Margueritte's cavalry charged the village of Floing three times, and he was mortally wounded in the first charge. With shellfire pouring in from all sides and every break-out defeated, Napoleon III had a white flag hoisted on the fortress wall. At 11:30 on 2 September Wimpffen signed the capitulation. The French lost 3,220 killed and 14,811 wounded, and 104,000 men passed into captivity with 558 guns. The emperor was sent on 3 September to Schloss Wilhelmshöhe near Kassel; when the news reached Paris, the empress is reported to have asked, "Why didn't he kill himself?" In Germany 2 September was celebrated as Sedantag every year until 1919. ## 4 September and the Government of National Defence {france}

News of the capitulation at Sedan reached Paris on the night of 3 September, and from the morning of the 4th crowds filled the Palais Bourbon, seat of the legislature, demanding a republic. That afternoon at the Hôtel de Ville, Léon Gambetta proclaimed the Republic: "The people has forestalled the Chamber which was wavering. To save the Nation in danger, it has asked for the Republic." The Second Empire fell without bloodshed. The new Government of National Defence was headed by General Louis-Jules Trochu, the military governor of Paris, with Jules Favre as vice-president and foreign minister and Gambetta as minister of the interior, and was filled out by the republican deputies elected for Paris, among them Jules Ferry, Jules Simon, Ernest Picard and Henri Rochefort. Trochu, an Orleanist, accepted the presidency on a promise that the government would "resolutely defend religion, property, and the family". Though several factions apart from the Bonapartists were represented, real power lay with the Orleanists and the conservatives. Only the United States and Spain recognised the government at once; Bismarck questioned whether a body made up solely of Parisians could speak for France, called Napoleon III "the legitimate ruler of France" and dismissed Gambetta's republic as "un coup de parti". [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Gambetta) [13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_National_Defense) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis-Jules_Trochu)

On 6 September Favre declared that France would not "yield an inch of its territory nor a stone of its fortresses", a phrase soon posted on walls all over Paris. Yet Favre, like Trochu, did not believe France could win the war; he opened a channel to Bismarck through the British ambassador Lord Lyons, and proposed to the cabinet that Germany be offered an indemnity in return for evacuating French soil, which was rejected. On 18 and 19 September he met Bismarck at the Château de Ferrières. Favre offered an indemnity of 500 million francs but refused any cession of territory; Bismarck demanded a frontier immune to a French war of revenge, including Strasbourg, Alsace and most of the Moselle department with Metz. When Bismarck asked for the surrender of Strasbourg and Toul as the price of an armistice for elections to a National Assembly, Favre wept and broke off, and on the 20th the cabinet rejected the terms completely. On the 24th the government postponed local and national elections indefinitely: in Gambetta's words, "We could not have elections without an armistice, and the effect of an armistice would be to relax the efforts of the defence." The republic renewed the declaration of war, called for recruits throughout the country and pledged to drive the Germans out by a guerre à outrance. Meanwhile the German armies were reducing the fortresses of Alsace. After Wörth, August von Werder took 40,000 Baden troops and Prussian Landwehr south to Strasbourg and began bombarding the city on 23 August. The museum of fine arts and the municipal library with its medieval manuscripts burned; the bishop begged for a ceasefire, but the elderly General Uhrich refused to surrender. Running short of shells, the Germans switched to a formal siege, breached the enceinte on 17 September, and the garrison, having learned of Sedan, capitulated on 28 September. The besiegers had fired 202,099 shells, about 4,000 tons; 341 civilians were killed and 10,000 left homeless. In his address of 9 September Marx wrote that Strasbourg "has for six days been wantonly and fiendishly bombarded". The fall of Strasbourg and Toul opened the railway from Germany to the siege lines of Paris, and Werder's corps moved south against Belfort. By 15 September the German armies had reached the outskirts of Paris and Moltke issued the orders for its investment; the ring closed on the 19th, and from the 20th Paris was cut off from the rest of France. ## The siege of Paris and the war in the provinces {france germany}

Paris had about 513,000 potential defenders: 60,000 regulars who had escaped from Sedan, 90,000 Mobiles, 13,000 naval seamen and 350,000 National Guards. The 33 km Thiers wall and sixteen detached forts built in the 1840s ringed the city. Moltke never intended to storm the city, and Blumenthal, who directed the siege, and the crown prince opposed a bombardment that would strike civilians; Bismarck, fearing the intervention of neutrals, pressed constantly for an early bombardment. Trochu had little faith in the National Guard, and his proclamation that the governor of Paris would never capitulate raised expectations doomed to disappointment. On 7 October Gambetta flew over the German lines in the coal-gas balloon Armand-Barbès and reached Tours, where as minister of the interior and of war, assisted by the engineer officer Charles de Freycinet, he governed unoccupied France as a virtual dictator. In less than four months eleven new army corps were formed, at an average of six thousand infantrymen and two batteries a day. The North German Confederation, which had mobilised 888,000 men in August, increased its forces by only 15 per cent by the end of the war, so that in November only the troops released by the fall of Metz saw the Germans through a crisis at the front. Fighting between German and republican forces began near Orléans on 10 October. The improvised Army of the Loire, made up of francs-tireurs, provincial Mobiles, naval units and zouaves from Algeria, gave up Orléans on the 11th but beat the Bavarians at Coulmiers on 9 November and retook the city. On 27 October, however, Bazaine had surrendered Metz and his starving army of 173,000 men (193,000 in some accounts), freeing Friedrich Karl's Second Army, and the German press reported widely on Bazaine's offer to "cooperate" against the "republican menace". Beaten at Beaune-la-Rolande on 28 November and Loigny on 2 December, the Army of the Loire lost Orléans again on 4 December, and the government delegation moved to Bordeaux. Gambetta split the army in two: Chanzy's Second Army of the Loire collapsed at Le Mans on 11–12 January 1871 with 7,000 killed and wounded, 22,000 captured and 50,000 deserters, while Faidherbe's Army of the North, after Amiens and Bapaume, was scattered at St. Quentin on 13 January. In besieged Paris, on 31 October, the day the surrender of Metz was confirmed, National Guard battalions led by Blanqui, Flourens and Delescluze seized the Hôtel de Ville and held Trochu's cabinet hostage before withdrawing overnight; despite a promise of no reprisals, the government arrested 22 of the leaders, embittering the Parisian left. Francs-tireurs cut railways and bridges and surprised small posts, but the Germans treated them as armed civilians without combatant status, shot those they captured and took reprisals on the nearest villages; at Bazeilles beside Sedan, Bavarian troops shot more than thirty inhabitants and burned the village. In Paris the diet moved from horsemeat to dogs, cats and rats and finally to the zoo's elephants, and by January three to four thousand people a week were dying of cold and hunger. The "great sortie" at Champigny on 30 November and the sortie towards Le Bourget on 21 December failed. From 5 January, as Bismarck wished, the Germans fired some 12,000 shells into the city over 23 nights, killing or wounding about 400, but the will to resist held. When the last sortie, against the château of Buzenval on 19 January, ended with more than 4,000 casualties, Trochu handed the governorship of Paris to General Vinoy on the 22nd, and a small rising on the 23rd was crushed by force. ## The First International and the German Social Democrats against the war {uk germany france}

The Second Empire had treated the International Working Men's Association as an enemy before the war began. On the eve of the plebiscite of May 1870 the government raided the association's administrative committees in Paris, Lyon, Rouen, Marseille and Brest on the pretext that it was a secret society plotting the emperor's assassination; at the trial of 22 June to 5 July the conspiracy charge collapsed, yet several members were jailed for their socialist beliefs alone. Because the French sections had told the people that a yes vote meant "despotism at home and war abroad", the workers of the great towns voted no almost as one, but the countryside tipped the balance. When the war crisis broke, the Paris members published a manifesto "to the Workmen of all Nations" in the Réveil of 12 July: "War for a question of preponderance or a dynasty can, in the eyes of workmen, be nothing but a criminal absurdity", and "Brothers in Germany! Our division would only result in the complete triumph of the despotism on both sides of the Rhine". Declarations from Neuilly-sur-Seine and elsewhere followed, and the prefect of police, Piétri, banned all street politics when the peace demonstrations of the working-class faubourgs grew too large. In Germany a mass meeting of workers at Brunswick on 16 July endorsed the Paris manifesto and declared "We are the enemies of all wars, but above all of dynastic wars"; at Chemnitz a meeting of delegates representing 50,000 Saxon workers called the war "exclusively dynastic"; and the Berlin branch replied that "neither the sound of the trumpets, nor the roar of the cannon, neither victory nor defeat, shall divert us from our common work". [25](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1871/civil-war-france/ch01.htm)

On 23 July the General Council in London issued its first address, written by Karl Marx. It called the "war plot of July 1870" an "amended edition of the coup d'état of December 1851" and predicted that "the death-knell of the Second Empire has already sounded at Paris. It will end, as it began, by a parody." On the German side the war was defensive, but what had put Germany in that position was Bismarck's Prussia, which had conspired with Bonaparte to crush opposition at home and annex Germany to the Hohenzollern dynasty; if the German working class allowed the war "to lose its strictly defensive character and to degenerate into a war against the French people, victory or defeat will prove alike disastrous". Russia loomed in the background, and the Germans would forfeit all sympathy the moment the Prussian government accepted "the help of the Cossack". In the Reichstag of the North German Confederation the two deputies of the Social Democratic Workers' Party, the Eisenachers August Bebel and Wilhelm Liebknecht, abstained in the vote on war credits on 21 July (19 July in the German-language source), a compromise Bebel devised so as neither to support the Prussian government nor to appear to favour Napoleon. The party's central committee in Brunswick, Wilhelm Bracke and Samuel Spier, who like Marx saw the first phase of the war as a legitimate defence against aggression, clashed fiercely with the two deputies who had refused a war "against brothers", and the year-old party came close to breaking apart. [25](https://www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1871/civil-war-france/ch01.htm) [26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bebel) [27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Liebknecht) [28](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braunschweiger_Manifest)

After Sedan the Brunswick committee too turned against continuing the war. In a letter to the committee of about 1 September, Marx and Engels overturned the claim that annexing Alsace-Lorraine would protect Germany from war for ever: it was "the best means of turning this war into a European institution", the surest way of perpetuating military despotism in the new Germany as the price of holding "a western Poland", and would turn the coming peace into "a mere armistice until France has recovered sufficiently to demand back her lost territories". On 5 September the committee issued its manifesto: "We protest against the annexation of Alsace and Lorraine. And we are conscious of speaking in the name of the German working class", demanding an "honourable peace" with the French republic and the extradition of Louis Bonaparte. On the orders of the commanding general Vogel von Falckenstein the manifesto was confiscated, and all the committee members, down to the printer, were arrested and taken "in chains like common criminals" to Lötzen in East Prussia, a thousand kilometres from Brunswick. Marx reported this in the Pall Mall Gazette on 15 September. The liberal Johann Jacoby was also imprisoned for protesting against the annexation. The General Council's second address of 9 September declared that "the war of defense ended, in point of fact, with the surrender of Louis Bonaparte, the Sedan capitulation, and the proclamation of the republic at Paris", refuted point by point the case for annexation as a "material guarantee", and argued that making military considerations the principle of national boundaries "carries within it the seed of fresh wars"; by driving France into the arms of Russia, annexation would lead to "a war of races", "with the Slavonic and Roman races". It hailed the republic while warning that the Orleanists held the army and the police; the French workers were told that any attempt to upset the new government with the enemy at the gates of Paris "would be a desperate folly", and to use republican liberty for their own class organisation. When the North German Reichstag took up further war credits on 26 November, Bebel and Liebknecht moved a peace proposal "renouncing any annexation of French territory" and voted against the credits. The debate turned into accusations of treason against the two deputies, followed by tumults and physical attacks, especially on Liebknecht. On 17 December the two were arrested together with Adolf Hepner, the second editor of the party organ Der Volksstaat. Liebknecht greeted unification under Prussian leadership with the slogan "For this system, not one man and not one penny!", which became the watchword of the party's opposition to the Bismarckian state. After Bebel won a seat in the election to the new German Reichstag on 3 March 1871, the government bowed to pressure and released the three on 28 March. In the Reichstag Bebel hailed the Paris Commune as a "preliminary skirmish" in the long campaign of the international working class. Since the war was over, no trial for Landesverrat (treason against the country) was possible; Bismarck pressed on, and the charge became Hochverrat (high treason). At the trial before the Leipzig jury court from 11 to 26 March 1872 Hepner was acquitted; Bebel and Liebknecht were found guilty by exactly the required minimum of eight jurors and sentenced to two years' fortress confinement, and Bebel was stripped of his seat. Liebknecht called himself "a soldier of the revolution" before the court, and because the prosecution had read the Communist Manifesto, then out of print, into the record, the Social Democrats could republish it legally. At the by-election of January 1873 Bebel was re-elected with more than 4,000 votes more than in the first round. ## The empire proclaimed at Versailles, and the armistice {germany france}

The victories of August and September drew the South German princes into the North German Confederation. In November 1870 Baden, Hesse, Württemberg and Bavaria signed treaties; on 8 December the Bundesrat voted to rename the Confederation the "German Empire" and to make the king of Prussia German Emperor, and on 9 and 10 December the Reichstag voted to offer the title. The new constitution came into force on 1 January 1871. Wilhelm I feared the imperial title would overshadow his Prussian crown and wanted to be "Kaiser von Deutschland", but Bismarck warned that the South German princes and the emperor of Austria would protest, and "Deutscher Kaiser" was settled on. The proclamation was fixed for 18 January, the anniversary of the coronation of the first Prussian king in 1701. That day the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles was crowded with delegations of the regiments holding their battle-torn colours; a field altar stood in place of a throne, a service was held, and Bismarck read out the proclamation. Grand Duke Friedrich of Baden, Wilhelm's only son-in-law, avoided the constitutional title and shouted "His Majesty, Kaiser Wilhelm", and those present repeated it three times. Wilhelm stressed the religious character of the ceremony, while Bismarck openly criticised the emperor for not seeing himself as holding authority over the princes but as a commander triumphing with his comrades. Held in the palace of the besieged enemy capital, the ceremony was remembered in France as a national humiliation. [32](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_German_Empire) [33](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_I,_German_Emperor) [3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_German_Confederation) [24](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsch-Franz%C3%B6sischer_Krieg)

Over the winter tensions grew within the German leadership. Moltke and Blumenthal wanted a methodical siege that would reduce the detached forts one by one; Bismarck wanted a quick end, fearing that a long siege would strain the economy, give France time to raise new armies and draw in the neutrals. On 25 January Wilhelm I overruled Moltke and ordered him to consult Bismarck on all future operations, and Bismarck at once had the city bombarded with large-calibre Krupp siege guns. Favre, empowered by the cabinet on 23 January to seek a general armistice, reached Versailles that evening. When he voiced his fear that the National Guard would rebel, Bismarck advised him to "provoke an uprising, then, while you still have an army with which to suppress it". The terms agreed were the surrender of the forts around Paris, the disarming of the regular troops less one division, the National Guard keeping its arms, an indemnity of 200 million francs, an armistice until 19 February and elections to a National Assembly. The guns fell silent at midnight on the 27th, and on 28 January Favre and Bismarck signed the convention. The departments of Jura, Doubs and Côte-d'Or were excluded at French request so as to preserve the fortified region of Belfort; Favre neglected to tell the government at Bordeaux, and the Army of the East under Clinchant, operating there, halted in the belief that the armistice applied and was surrounded by Manteuffel's Army of the South. On 1 February the last French army, 87,000 men, crossed from Pontarlier through Les Verrières into Switzerland, where it was disarmed and interned. The National Guard's retention of its arms later made the rising of the Paris Commune possible. In Bordeaux, Gambetta received the news of the surrender by telegram on 29 January, was furious and refused to accept it. On 6 February Gambetta resigned and handed the provincial armies to the government. The elections of 8 February, held with 43 departments under occupation and all public meetings banned so that only Paris saw a campaign, returned a large majority of Legitimists and Orleanists pledged to peace. Gambetta was elected in eight departments, but Thiers was returned simultaneously in many constituencies (23 or 86, depending on the source). The Assembly met in Bordeaux on 12 February, made Thiers chief executive, and on the 19th its members swore the "Pact of Bordeaux", a truce that left the question of republic or monarchy open. The preliminary peace was signed at Versailles on 26 February; on 1 March 30,000 Prussian, Bavarian and Saxon troops paraded through a silent Paris draped in black and withdrew after two days to encampments east of the city. The same day the National Assembly formally declared the emperor deposed and placed the blame for the defeat on him. Once peace was arranged Bismarck released Napoleon III, who crossed to England on 20 March, settled at Chislehurst in Kent and died on 9 January 1873 after operations for bladder stones; his last words are reported as "Isn't it true that we weren't cowards at Sedan?" ## The Treaty of Frankfurt and Alsace-Lorraine {france germany}

On 10 May 1871 the German Empire and the French Republic signed the peace treaty at Frankfurt. France ceded the Alsatian departments of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin, except Belfort and its territory, and in Lorraine most of the Moselle department, a third of Meurthe including Château-Salins and Sarrebourg, and the cantons of Saales and Schirmeck in the Vosges: 1,694 villages and towns, 1,447,000 hectares and 1,597,000 inhabitants, together with 20 per cent of France's mining and steel potential. The inhabitants had until 1 October 1872 to opt for French nationality and emigrate, or to stay and become German citizens. The indemnity was five billion francs in gold, payable within five years; one billion had to be paid in 1871 before any German withdrawal, and parts of France remained occupied until the sum was paid in full. The figure was proportioned by population to be the exact equivalent of the indemnity Napoleon I had imposed on Prussia in 1807. France recognised Wilhelm I as German Emperor. France paid the indemnity faster than agreed, and the German troops withdrew in September 1873. The German military regarded Alsace up to the Vosges and the route between Thionville and Metz as essential for any future war with France. The new border largely followed the linguistic one, but the annexation of French-speaking Metz caused outrage in France, and resources such as iron and coal do not appear to have motivated the annexation. [35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Frankfurt_%281871%29) [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War)

On 28 June 1871 the annexed land became the "Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine", not a constituent state but a territory governed directly by a governor appointed by the emperor. Prussia held that the population first had to be "Germanised" and initially treated the region as occupied territory. About 90 per cent of the inhabitants spoke German dialects, but Catholics were sceptical of unification under Protestant Prussia, and when the Kulturkampf reached the territory in 1872–73 the Catholic Church became a vehicle of resistance. 160,878 people, 10.4 per cent of the population and 20.3 per cent in Upper Alsace, opted for French nationality, though only about 50,000 actually left for France; some estimates put the optants as high as 280,000 and those who left at 130,000. When the territory received 15 Reichstag seats in 1874, between six and ten of those elected were "protest deputies" opposed to the annexation; their French-language motion asking that "the population of Alsace-Lorraine, which has been incorporated into the German Empire by the Treaty of Frankfurt without having been consulted, be called upon to express its opinion on this annexation" was rejected by a large majority. Nor was the population consulted when it returned to France in 1918. Whether Bismarck wanted the annexation or was pushed into it by the army and a wave of public opinion is debated among historians; his biographers hold that he "reluctantly gave in", and count the annexation his main mistake, because it turned France into a permanent enemy. [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace%E2%80%93Lorraine) [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck) [35](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Frankfurt_%281871%29)

Germany sent 33,101 officers and 1,113,254 men into France and lost 28,306 in battle (17,585 killed in action and 10,721 dead of wounds), with 12,147 more dead of disease, 6,965 of them from typhoid; 89,732 were wounded. French battle deaths were 77,000 (41,000 killed and 36,000 dead of wounds) and more than 45,000 died of sickness, for a total of 138,871 dead; 137,626 were wounded and 383,860 taken prisoner, while 90,192 were interned in Switzerland and 6,300 in Belgium. Prussian executions of prisoners (more than 200 French soldiers at Dornach) and violence against civilians were also recorded. The war was over, but the fight for Paris was not. During the siege the National Guard of the working-class districts had become politicised enough to elect its officers and refuse orders from the national government, and on 18 March 1871, when regular troops tried to remove the cannon on Montmartre, it resisted and killed two generals. The government and the army withdrew to Versailles and a Commune was set up in Paris. In the Bloody Week of 21–28 May the regular army retook the city; the Communards killed by government troops were long estimated at between 7,000 and 30,000, and more recent studies of cemetery burials put the figure at 6,000 to 10,000. The survivors were amnestied in 1880 by a bill introduced by Gambetta. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_Versailles)

## Assessment {france germany}

Accounts of the war's origins still diverge. Bismarck himself fed the myth of a master plan by writing in his memoirs that he "always considered that a war with France would naturally follow a war against Austria", and some historians hold that he deliberately provoked France to bring in the South German states. Others argue that the Ems dispatch played only a minor role and that Napoleon III had already chosen war because he believed he would win, while the French historians François Roth and Pierre Milza see the emperor as pushed by a bellicose press and public opinion. In Germany the character of the war is debated. Tobias Arand treats the war up to Sedan as a classic cabinet war, transformed afterwards by the Government of National Defence's mobilisation of civilians and by the German demands for territory. Alexander Seyferth classes it as a stage on the road to the total wars of the twentieth century because of the mobilisation and propaganda of the home front, while Christine Krüger objects that the home front is only one feature of total war among many, and that the humane treatment of prisoners and the relatively quick end of the confrontation set it apart from the world wars. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ems_Dispatch) [5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck) [24](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsch-Franz%C3%B6sischer_Krieg) [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III)

The figures vary by source. The force that surrendered at Metz is given as 173,000 in the overview article and as 193,000 in the article on the siege (6,000 officers and 167,000 men taken prisoner, with 20,000 sick left behind). The French strength at Gravelotte is 112,800, while the Napoleon III article puts Bazaine's army shut up in Metz at 175,000. For Alsace-Lorraine the official count of 160,878 optants for French nationality stands beside estimates of up to 280,000. Thiers is said to have been elected in 23 or in 86 constituencies in February 1871; the date of Bebel's and Liebknecht's abstention on war credits is 21 July in the English source and 19 July in the German one, and their arrest is dated December 1871 in the English Bebel article but 17 December 1870 in the Liebknecht article and the German article on the trial. For the Commune the traditional estimate of 7,000 to 30,000 dead confronts the 6,000 to 10,000 of studies of burial records. This account gives the range at each point. [1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War) [10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Metz_%281870%29) [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III) [36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alsace%E2%80%93Lorraine) [34](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1871_French_legislative_election) [12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Gambetta) [26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Bebel) [27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Liebknecht) [31](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipziger_Hochverratsprozess)

For the socialist movement the war left two precedents. The first was that the workers' organisations of the two belligerents exchanged messages of peace, and that the General Council, having denounced the "dynastic war" in two addresses, opposed the victor's annexation the moment the war lost its defensive character. Marx went beyond the German workers' critique of "material guarantees" to foresee that annexation would drive France into the arms of Russia and bring on a "war of races", "with the Slavonic and Roman races", and called the unified German Empire "a military despotism cloaked in parliamentary forms". Later historians likewise count the annexation Bismarck's main mistake, though they note that revanchism faded in the 1880s and that the recovery of Alsace-Lorraine became a French war aim only after the First World War had begun. The second precedent was the vote in parliament. The abstention and the no vote of Bebel and Liebknecht, the chains of the Brunswick committee and the fortress sentences of Leipzig made "not one man and not one penny for this system" the watchword of German Social Democracy, and once German nationalism after 1871 defined itself against France and by excluding the "enemies of the Reich" (Poles, Danes, Catholics and Social Democrats), the watchword became the party's identity. Yet the same Bebel supported the military budget of 1913 on condition of a property tax, foreshadowing the vote for war credits in 1914; the precedent of 1870 was not kept in 1914.
